notes: The text says to power the sensor from 3V3, but the circuit image (the authority) connects VCC to the Pi's 5V pin and uses a two-resistor voltage divider on the Echo line, so I followed the image.

The image shows the sensor in breadboard columns 1-4 of the row f-j half. The breadboard catalogue calls that half bank 'b' (rows f-j), so I used ports like '1b.j'. The lower a-e half is bank 't', e.g. '4t.c'.

Voltage divider: Echo (3b.f) goes by blue wire to 4t.d, then r1 (330 ohm, 4t.c to 8t.c) to the junction strip in column 8. A blue wire from 8t.e takes the junction to GPIO17. r2 (470 ohm, 8t.b to 12t.b) goes to GND through a black wire from 12t.a to rail bn.12. Resistor values are read from the colour bands and may be slightly off.
Rail hole numbers (bn.12, bn.24, bn.28) are estimated from where the holes sit relative to the column numbers in the image. I assumed the lower '-' rail is 'bn'.

Pi pin mapping from the image: the red wire goes to the top-left pin (5V.1), the green wire to GPIO4 (Trig) and the blue wire to GPIO17 (Echo). The black wire goes to the GND pin next to GPIO21, which I took as GND.8 (physical pin 39).

The buzzer image (circuit_2) was not provided. I followed the text: the buzzer connects directly to the Pi with two female jumper leads, one to GPIO21 and one to a GND pin. I assumed buzzer pin 1 is positive, and I chose GND.7 for the second lead.
The text says the sensor uses GPIO 27 for Trig in some places and 4 in others. The image shows GPIO4 (GP4), so I used that.
The Python code is not part of the physical build graph.
